teile.einleitung: A kite is a light flying object made of a frame and fabric or paper that flies in the wind on a string. Many children fly kites in autumn. Kites are an ancient toy, but they are also used for sport, science and festivals.
wichtigste: A kite needs wind to rise.
You hold it on a string.
Kites were invented a very long time ago in China.
A long tail makes a simple kite fly steadily.
You can build a simple kite yourself from wooden sticks and paper.
A stunt kite has two strings and can be steered.
In kitesurfing, a kite pulls a person on a board across the water.

abschnitte.text: A kite consists of a light **frame** made of wood, bamboo or plastic rods. Paper, plastic film or fabric is stretched over it; this is the **cover**. You hold the kite in the wind on a string. Because it hangs on the string, it cannot simply fly away. Modern kites are mostly made of nylon fabric with carbon fibre rods.

The kite stands at an angle in the wind. The air flows against the cover and pushes the kite upwards, creating **lift**. The string holds it in place; otherwise it would simply be blown away. On simple kites, a long **tail** makes sure it flies steadily and does not spin. Without wind a kite falls down, and in a storm it can tear.

Kites were invented a very long time ago in **China**, probably more than 2,000 years ago. There they were used for festivals, but also to send messages. Kites later reached Europe by way of Asia. In 1752 the American scientist **Benjamin Franklin** flew a kite into a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electrical. This experiment was very dangerous and must never be copied.

The classic **single-line kite** has the shape of a diamond and a single string. A **stunt kite** has two strings with which you can steer it and fly tricks. Box kites are three-dimensional and fly very steadily. Huge kites in the shape of animals can be seen at kite festivals, for example in Asia or on North Sea beaches.

In **kitesurfing**, a large stunt kite pulls a person on a board across the water. In Switzerland you can watch this, for example, on Lake Silvaplana in the Engadine, where a strong wind often blows. In winter there is also snowkiting, where you are pulled on skis or a snowboard. Kite sportspeople can even make high jumps with their kites.

You can build a simple kite yourself from two **wooden sticks** and paper. You tie the sticks together into a cross and stretch a string all the way round. Then you glue paper over it and attach a tail made of paper bows. Here people like to fly kites in autumn, because it is often windy then. You should always stay far away from power lines, roads and airfields.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that pushes an object upwards in the air.
Kite with two strings that you can steer.
The fabric, paper or plastic film over the frame.
Water sport in which a kite pulls a person on a board.

gewusst: In China kites were built more than 2,000 years ago.
The Wright brothers first tested their ideas for the aeroplane on large kites.
On Lake Silvaplana in the Engadine, people often kite thanks to the regular Maloja wind.

teile.einleitung: Empa is the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology. It examines materials such as concrete, metals, plastics and textiles and develops new materials and technologies. It belongs to the ETH Domain and has sites in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.
wichtigste: Empa stands for Eidgenössische Materialprüfungs- und Forschungsanstalt, the Federal Materials Testing and Research Institute.
Its forerunner was founded in Zurich in 1880 as an institute for testing building materials.
Empa works in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.
It belongs to the ETH Domain.
In 1891 the young testing institute under Ludwig von Tetmajer investigated the collapse of the railway bridge near Münchenstein.
Its main areas include nanostructured materials and technologies.
On the “move” platform in Dübendorf, mobility without fossil fuels has been tested since 2015.
In 2022 Tanja Zimmermann became the first woman to head Empa.

abschnitte.text: Empa is a research institute of the Swiss Confederation. It tests how strong, durable or safe materials are and looks for new, better materials. It works closely with companies, universities and authorities. It belongs to the **ETH Domain**, together with ETH Zurich, EPFL and other research institutes.

In 1880 an **institute for testing building materials** was set up in Zurich, the forerunner of Empa. At that time many bridges and railway lines were being built, and people wanted to be sure that iron and cement would hold. In 1891 a railway bridge collapsed under a train near **Münchenstein** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. Under **Ludwig von Tetmajer**, the testing institute investigated the collapse, which greatly increased its importance.

The largest site is in **Dübendorf** near Zurich. In **St Gallen**, Empa researches among other things textiles and materials for medicine and health. In **Thun** the work is, for example, on surfaces and joining techniques. Experts from physics, chemistry, engineering and biology work together there.

One focus is **nanostructured materials**, that is, substances with tiny structures a thousand times thinner than a hair. Other topics are energy, sustainable building, the environment and health. Empa also measures air pollutants and studies how materials age. In this way it helps to make products safer and more environmentally friendly.

In Dübendorf, Empa has test facilities where new ideas are tried out under real conditions. On the **move** platform, opened in 2015, mobility without fossil fuels is tested, for example with hydrogen or electricity. In the **NEST** research building, new building and energy technologies are tested directly in lived-in flats and offices. In this way research results reach everyday life faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: Examining how strong, durable and safe a material is.
Group made up of the two Swiss Federal Institutes of Technology and several federal research institutes.
Material with tiny structures in the range of millionths of a millimetre.
Fuels made from oil, natural gas or coal.

gewusst: The Münchenstein bridge collapse of 1891 is considered one of the worst railway accidents in Switzerland.
In the NEST research building, individual living units can be swapped like drawers.
Among other things, Empa tests whether protective clothing really protects against heat or cold.

teile.einleitung: District heating is heat produced at a central place and delivered to many buildings through a network of pipes. It is used to heat flats and warm water. In Switzerland much district heating comes from waste incineration plants, wood or waste heat.
wichtigste: District heating is produced centrally and delivered to many buildings through pipes.
It usually flows as hot water in well-insulated pipes.
In many Swiss cities, waste incineration plants supply a large share of the district heating.
In the house, a heat exchanger passes the heat on to the building's own heating.
A house with district heating needs no boiler of its own and no oil tank.
The Refuna district heating network in the lower Aare valley uses heat from the Beznau nuclear power station.
In rural heating networks, wood chips are often used for heating.

abschnitte.text: Instead of every house having its own heating, the heat is produced at a central place. From there it flows through a **district heating network** to homes, schools, hospitals and companies. The network can supply a few houses or whole parts of a city. In Switzerland smaller networks are often called **heating networks** (Wärmeverbund). The heat is used for heating and hot water.

abschnitte.titel: How the heat gets into the house
abschnitte.text: Usually hot water is pumped through thick, well-**insulated pipes** under the street. In the cellar of every connected house there is a **heat exchanger**. There the hot water gives off its heat to the house's heating water, without the two mixing. The cooled water flows back to the central plant and is heated up again. This creates a cycle like the blood in the body.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the heat come from?
abschnitte.text: In many Swiss cities such as Zurich, Bern or Basel, **waste incineration plants** supply a large share of the district heating. Burning rubbish produces a lot of heat that would otherwise be lost. Such heat, produced as a by-product of a process, is called **waste heat**. Industrial plants, data centres and sewage treatment works also give off waste heat. In the countryside, many heating networks use **wood chips** from their own forests.

In the lower Aare valley in the canton of Aargau there is the **Refuna** district heating network. It uses heat from the Beznau nuclear power station. A network of pipes connects several municipalities in the region with the power station. In this way heat is used that is produced anyway when generating electricity.

A house with district heating needs no **boiler** of its own and no oil tank. This saves space in the cellar, and there are fewer exhaust fumes in the neighbourhood. If the heat comes from rubbish, wood or waste heat, it is better for the climate than heating oil. But building a district heating network is expensive, because streets have to be dug up. That is why it is worthwhile mainly where many houses stand close together.

Many Swiss cities are currently greatly expanding their district heating networks. In this way they want to replace oil and gas heating and cut emissions of **CO₂**. Some networks also use heat from lakes, rivers or groundwater with large heat pumps. When you see big roadworks with thick pipes in the street, district heating is often being laid.

begriffe.erklaerung: Device that passes heat from one water circuit to another without them mixing.
Heat produced as a by-product of a process.
Smaller network that supplies several buildings together with heat.
Plant in which rubbish is burned and the heat is used for electricity and heating.

gewusst: In many cities, the rubbish we throw away becomes heat for thousands of flats.
The pipes of a district heating network are so well insulated that the water cools only a little on the way.
Even the waste heat from computers in data centres can heat houses.

teile.einleitung: A number trick is a calculating stunt that at first looks like magic. But behind it there are always simple rules of mathematics. With number tricks you can amaze your friends or calculate faster in your head.
wichtigste: Many number tricks work with any starting number at all.
In the mind-reading trick, after doubling, adding 10, halving and subtracting the starting number, the answer is always 5.
A three-digit number written twice in a row is always divisible by 1001.
In the 1089 trick the result is always 1089.
With a trick you can multiply numbers by 11 in a flash in your head.
The Kaprekar constant 6174 appears for almost all four-digit numbers.
If you know the algebra behind a trick, you can explain it and invent your own.

abschnitte.text: Ask someone to think of a number, double it, add 10, halve the result and subtract the number they thought of. The result is always 5. The reason: x becomes 2x + 10, halved x + 5, and after subtracting x, 5 is left. With a **variable** such as x you can see through such tricks and prove them.

When multiplying a two-digit number by 11, you write the sum of the digits in the middle. For 23 · 11 you write 2, then 2 + 3 = 5, then 3, giving 253. Numbers ending in 5 are squared like this: multiply the tens digit by the next number up and add 25 on the end. For 35 · 35 you work out 3 · 4 = 12 and add 25, which gives **1225**.

Take a three-digit number whose first and last digits differ by at least 2, for example 732. Subtract the **reversed number**: 732 − 237 = 495. Then add the reverse of the result: 495 + 594 = 1089. Whichever suitable number you start with, the answer at the end is always 1089.

In the 20th century the Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar discovered a special number. You arrange the digits of a four-digit number that is not made of all the same digits in descending and ascending order and subtract the smaller number from the larger. If you repeat this, you reach **6174** in at most seven steps. After that you stay there, because 7641 − 1467 gives 6174 again.

Some calculations give amazing patterns. 37 · 3 = 111, 37 · 6 = 222 and 37 · 9 = 333. Even more impressive is 12345679 · 9 = 111111111. If you write a three-digit number twice, such as 347347, it is the same as 347 · **1001**, and because 1001 = 7 · 11 · 13, the number is also divisible by 7, 11 and 13.

Number tricks are fun and show that mathematics is not only made of worksheets. If you want to explain a trick, you automatically learn **algebra**, that is calculating with letters. Mental arithmetic tricks help in everyday life, for example when shopping or estimating. Many magicians also use mathematical tricks for card tricks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A letter such as x that stands for any number.
The number you get when you read the digits backwards, for example 237 for 732.
The number 6174, at which Kaprekar’s trick always ends.
The part of mathematics in which you calculate with letters and equations.

gewusst: For three-digit numbers there is a similar Kaprekar number, namely 495.
The mind-reading trick also works with fractions and negative numbers.

teile.einleitung: A parachute is a large canopy made of fabric that brings a falling person or a load gently to the ground. It does this by using the resistance of the air. Without parachutes, parachute jumps, rescues from aircraft and many landings of space capsules would be impossible.
wichtigste: A parachute slows the fall because the air pushes against the large canopy.
The canopy is made of light but very strong fabric, usually nylon.
In 1797 André-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a balloon in Paris and landed with a parachute.
Parachutists always carry a second parachute as a reserve.
You open the canopy while you are still high enough above the ground.
Many space capsules slow down with parachutes shortly before landing.
The paraglider is a relative of the parachute with which you can take off from mountains and fly for a long time.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who jumps out of an aircraft falls faster and faster until the **air resistance** is as great as the force of gravity. Without a canopy a person reaches about 200 kilometres per hour this way. When the parachute opens, the surface suddenly becomes much larger and the air brakes strongly. After that you sink at only a few metres per second, about as fast as jumping off a wall. This speed is called the **rate of descent**.

A parachute consists of the **canopy**, many thin lines and the harness in which the jumper sits. The canopy is sewn from light, tear-resistant fabric such as nylon. Silk used to be used. Modern sports parachutes are rectangular wings made of two layers of fabric that fill with air. With two steering lines you can steer them and land gently.

As early as around 1485, the artist and inventor **Leonardo da Vinci** drew a parachute shaped like a pyramid. In 1797 the Frenchman André-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a balloon in Paris and landed safely with a parachute. Later parachutes became important for rescuing pilots from aircraft. Today parachuting is also a popular sport.

Every parachutist carries a **main parachute** and a **reserve parachute**. If the main parachute does not open properly, you can cut it away and pull the second one. Many jumpers also have a small device that opens the reserve automatically if you are too low. The canopy must be opened while you are still high enough above the ground. Beginners often jump first as a tandem with an experienced instructor.

Space capsules coming back from space slow down with huge parachutes shortly before landing. Racing aircraft and dragsters sometimes use **drag chutes** too. Aid supplies are dropped from aircraft with parachutes. In nature, dandelion seeds fly through the air on tiny umbrellas, far away from the parent plant.

The **paraglider** looks similar to a parachute but is built for flying. You take off on foot on a mountain slope and can fly for hours in rising warm air. Paragliding is very popular in Switzerland, for example above Interlaken or in Valais. Many tourists take a tandem flight with a pilot there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air slows down a moving object.
The actual fabric parachute that fills with air.
A second parachute for emergencies.
A jump in which a guest is attached to an experienced jumper.
A steerable wing with which you take off from a mountain and fly for a long time.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci drew a parachute more than 300 years before anyone really jumped with one.
Without a parachute a person falls as fast as a car on the motorway, even faster.
Dandelion seeds work on the same principle as a parachute.

teile.einleitung: Fly-by-wire is a control system for aircraft in which the pilot's commands are sent electrically via computers to the control surfaces. In the past the control columns were connected directly to the control surfaces by cables and rods. Today almost all modern airliners and fighter aircraft fly with fly-by-wire.
wichtigste: With fly-by-wire, control commands are sent electrically via computers to the control surfaces.
Concorde already had an analogue fly-by-wire system.
The Airbus A320 was the first airliner with fully digital fly-by-wire controls.
The General Dynamics F-16 was the first mass-produced fighter aircraft with fly-by-wire.
In Airbus cockpits a sidestick replaces the classic control yoke.
Flight envelope protection prevents dangerous flight situations such as a stall.
Several independent computers make sure that a single failure is not dangerous.
With fly-by-light, the signals travel through fibre-optic cables.

abschnitte.text: The English expression means roughly “flying by wire”. When the pilot moves the control stick, the movement is converted into electrical **signals**. These go to **flight control computers**, which calculate how the control surfaces should move. Electric or hydraulic actuators then move the elevators, ailerons and rudder. There is usually no longer a direct mechanical connection.

In older aircraft, the control stick and control surfaces were connected by **control cables**, rods and pulleys. This technology is heavy and needs frequent maintenance. Electrical lines are lighter, and the computer can fine-tune the aircraft's movements. **Concorde**, which flew in scheduled service from 1976, already had an analogue fly-by-wire system. At the end of the 1980s the **Airbus A320** was the first airliner with fully digital controls.

In Airbus cockpits there is no longer a large control yoke in front of the pilot. Instead there is a small **sidestick** at the side, similar to a joystick in computer games. The captain steers with the left hand, the co-pilot with the right. This leaves room in front of the pilots for a fold-out table. Boeing, on the other hand, still uses a control yoke in its fly-by-wire aircraft.

The computers constantly monitor whether the aircraft is flying safely. **Flight envelope protection** prevents dangerous situations, such as climbing too steeply, turning too sharply or a **stall**. Because the controls are so important, there are several computers independent of each other. If one fails, the others take over, so a single failure does not lead to loss of control. This is called **redundancy**.

The American **General Dynamics F-16** was the first mass-produced fighter aircraft with fly-by-wire. Many modern fighter jets are deliberately built to be slightly unstable so that they are very agile. Without computers making corrections many times every second, a human could not fly them at all. The Swiss Air Force's F/A-18 also has fly-by-wire controls.

A further development is called **fly-by-light**. Here the control signals travel as light signals through fibre-optic cables instead of copper wires. Optical fibres are even lighter and are not affected by electrical interference, for example from a lightning strike. So far this technology is used in only a few aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small control stick at the side of the pilot's seat.
Dangerous situation in which the wings suddenly stop producing lift.
Systems present more than once, so that if one part fails another takes over.
Movable flaps on the aircraft with which it is steered.
Control system in which the signals travel through fibre-optic cables.

gewusst: Many modern fighter aircraft could not be kept stable in the air by any human without computer help.
Some modern cars already steer electrically; this is called steer-by-wire.
The sidestick in an Airbus is operated with only one hand.

teile.einleitung: The foundation is the lowest part of a building, which sits in the ground and carries all the weight. Later you hardly see it, but without a foundation a house would sink, become crooked or even collapse. That is why it is always built first.
wichtigste: A foundation spreads the weight of the house over the ground so that it does not sink.
The foundation is built first, even before the walls.
Today foundations are mostly made of concrete, often reinforced with steel.
A skyscraper needs an especially strong foundation, because it is very heavy.
Foundations must lie deep enough so that frost does not damage them.
Many old houses in Venice stand on wooden piles.
The saying “built on sand” means that something is unsafe.

abschnitte.text: A **foundation** is the part of a structure that carries the whole load down into the **subsoil**. This includes the weight of the walls, ceilings and roof, but also furniture, people and snow on the roof. The foundation spreads this weight over a large area, rather like snowshoes that stop you sinking into the snow. Without this spreading, the house would press into the ground and crack.

Under single columns a **pad foundation** is built, under walls a long strip foundation. Many modern houses stand on a **raft**, a thick concrete slab under the whole building. If the ground is soft, long **piles** are driven or drilled deep into the earth until they reach firm ground. Such pile foundations even carry very tall towers and large bridges.

Today foundations are mostly made of **concrete**, a mixture of cement, sand, gravel and water that sets rock-hard. To stop it breaking, steel bars are placed inside; this is then called **reinforced concrete**. The ancient Romans already knew a kind of concrete and built huge structures with it. Earlier houses often had foundations of stacked natural stones.

When wet soil freezes, the water in it expands and can lift and damage a foundation. That is why a foundation must lie deeper than the frost line, in Switzerland often about 80 centimetres to more than a metre deep, and even deeper in the mountains. Before building, experts examine the ground carefully; this is called a **geological survey**. In areas with earthquakes, such as Valais or near Basel, buildings are also made earthquake-resistant.

Many houses in **Venice** stand on millions of wooden piles stuck in the muddy ground of the lagoon. Under water and without air the wood hardly rots, so it has lasted for centuries. The **Leaning Tower of Pisa**, on the other hand, started to tilt while it was still being built, because its foundation on soft ground was not deep enough. That is why the saying “built on sand” means that something is unsafe and could easily collapse.

begriffe.erklaerung: Lowest part of a structure, which carries the weight down into the ground.
The ground on which a building stands.
Concrete with steel bars set inside it, which is especially stable.
Foundation made of long piles that reach down to firm ground.
Depth down to which the ground can freeze in winter.

gewusst: The foundations of very tall skyscrapers often reach several dozen metres deep into the ground.
Wood lasts so long under water because fungi and bacteria can hardly work without oxygen.
The word “foundation” comes from the Latin “fundus”, which means “bottom” or “ground”.

teile.einleitung: The angle bisector is a line that divides an angle into two exactly equal parts. Every point on it is the same distance from both arms. It can be constructed very precisely with compasses and a ruler.
wichtigste: The angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts.
An angle of 74° becomes two angles of 37° each.
All the points on it are the same distance from both arms.
It is the line of symmetry of the two arms.
The construction starts with an arc around the vertex.
A triangle has three bisectors of its interior angles; they meet at the centre of the incircle.
The bisectors of two adjacent angles on a line are perpendicular to each other.

abschnitte.text: The **angle bisector** passes through the vertex of an angle and divides it exactly in the middle. If an angle measures 74°, two angles of 37° each are formed. With a right angle, two angles of 45° are formed. You can imagine folding the angle exactly down the middle.

The angle bisector is the **line of symmetry** of the two arms. If you reflect one arm in it, it lands exactly on the other. That is why every point on the angle bisector is the same **distance** from both arms. This property is used in many constructions.

First you draw an **arc** with the compasses around the vertex, cutting both arms. Around these two points of intersection you now draw two arcs of the same size, which cross inside the angle. The line from the vertex through this crossing point is the angle bisector. This makes it more accurate than with a set square alone.

A triangle has three interior angles and therefore three angle bisectors. They all meet at one point, the centre of the **incircle**. The incircle is the largest circle that fits inside the triangle and touches all three sides. In an equilateral triangle this point coincides with the centre of the circumcircle.

In a square the bisector of a corner angle is a diagonal. Two adjacent angles on a line add up to 180°, so their bisectors form a right angle of 90°. The line y = x in the coordinate system is also an angle bisector, namely that of the two axes. In practice, carpenters, for example, use the angle bisector when they join two strips of wood exactly in a corner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line that divides an angle into two equal halves.
The point where the two arms of an angle meet.
A circle inside a triangle that touches all three sides.
A line in which a shape can be reflected onto itself.

gewusst: The corners of a picture frame are often cut at an angle of 45°, that is exactly along the angle bisector.
Bisecting an angle with compasses and a ruler is easy, but dividing it exactly into three is in general impossible with them.
You can also find the angle bisector by folding a piece of paper.

teile.einleitung: The landline is the telephone network in which a telephone is permanently connected to a line in the house. Long before there were mobile phones, everyone made calls over the landline. Many households and companies still have a landline connection today.
wichtigste: A landline telephone is connected to a fixed line in the house.
On old telephones you dialled the number with a rotary dial.
When making a call you hold the handset to your ear.
If you pick up the handset and the line is free, you hear a humming tone.
The area code shows the region; 031, for example, stands for Bern.
In the past all telephone numbers were listed in the thick telephone directory.
When out and about, people made calls from a telephone box.
In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118.

abschnitte.text: With a landline, the telephone is connected to the telephone network by a line. The line runs from the house via cables to the **telephone exchange**. By contrast, a mobile phone works by radio in the **mobile network**. Because the telephone is attached to the line, you can only use it at home or in the office. Many landline telephones today, however, are cordless and have a base station.

A classic telephone consists of the unit and the **handset**, which you hold to your ear. Inside the handset are a small loudspeaker and a microphone. On old telephones you dialled the number with a **rotary dial**, which you had to turn for each digit. Later buttons were added. If you pick up the handset and the line is free, you hear a humming tone, the dialling tone.

Swiss landline numbers begin with an **area code** that shows the region. 031 stands for the Bern region, 044 for Zurich and 022 for Geneva. After that come seven more digits. In the past all numbers were listed with name and address in the thick **telephone directory**. Important emergency numbers are 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for the ambulance.

Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone in 1876. Soon telephone lines were built in many cities. At first, female operators connected the calls by hand with plugs. Later automatic exchanges took over this work. When out and about, people made calls from a **telephone box** with coins or a Taxcard.

Today landline calls in Switzerland mostly run digitally over the internet; this is called **IP telephony**. For this the telephone is connected to the router. Most public telephone boxes have disappeared because almost everyone has a mobile phone. Nevertheless many companies, hospitals and older people still use the landline. It is considered reliable and often has good sound quality.

begriffe.erklaerung: Part of the telephone you hold to your ear, with a loudspeaker and a microphone.
Turning disc on old telephones with which you dialled the number.
The first digits of a telephone number, which show the region.
Humming tone that shows the line is free.
Small booth with a public telephone.

gewusst: In the past, operators connected every call by hand with a plug.
With a rotary dial, dialling a 0 took longest, because you had to turn it furthest.
An old telephone directory for a big city listed hundreds of thousands of names.

teile.einleitung: Cube buildings are structures made of cubes of the same size, stacked next to and on top of each other. At school they are used to learn how to work out amounts and to picture three-dimensional solids. You look at them from the front, from the side and from above and draw building plans for them.
wichtigste: A cube building consists of many cubes of the same size.
You can find the number of cubes by counting, adding or multiplying.
A large cube made of 2 by 2 by 2 small cubes needs 8 cubes.
A building plan shows the view from above with a number on each square.
The number on a square says how many cubes are stacked there.
From above you cannot see well how tall a building is.
Cube buildings train spatial awareness.

abschnitte.text: A cube building is a solid made entirely of **cubes** of the same size. The cubes lie face to face, so not at a slant or out of line. You can build towers, walls, stairs or whole houses. At school, wooden cubes, linking cubes or building blocks are used for this.

With simple buildings you just count: a tower of 4 cubes with 2 more on top has 6 cubes. With regular shapes **multiplication** helps: a wall of 2 rows of 3 cubes each has 2 · 3 = 6 cubes, and 3 towers of 4 cubes each need 12 cubes. A staircase 1, 2 and 3 cubes high has 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 cubes. A large cube made of 2 · 2 · 2 small cubes needs 8, and one made of 3 · 3 · 3 already 27.

A cube building looks different from every side. A distinction is made between the **front view**, the side view and the plan view from above. From above you can see which squares are occupied, but not how tall the building is. That is why you often need several views to understand a building exactly. Cubes hidden right at the back or inside cannot be seen from any direction.

A **building plan** shows the building from above as a grid of squares. On each square you write a number that says how many cubes are stacked there. If you add up all the numbers, you know the total number of cubes. With such a plan someone else can rebuild the building exactly.

Many puzzle games are based on cube buildings. The **Soma cube** consists of seven pieces that can be put together to form a large cube of 27 small cubes. Construction sets with interlocking bricks and computer games with block worlds work in a similar way. Such games develop imagination and logical thinking.

If you understand cube buildings, you can picture solids in space better. This is needed later by, for example, architects, engineers, draughtspeople and tradespeople who build from plans. Spatial thinking also helps when packing a car boot or filling a shelf. In the Swiss primary school curriculum, cube buildings belong to the area of shape and space.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid with six square faces of equal size.
The view of a solid directly from above.
A drawing from above that shows how many cubes are stacked on each square.
The ability to picture solids and their position in space in your head.

gewusst: For a large cube with 10 small cubes along each edge you already need 1000 small cubes.
The Soma cube was thought up in 1933 by the Danish inventor Piet Hein.
From only two views you can sometimes build several different buildings that look exactly the same.

teile.einleitung: A shape-memory alloy is a metal that can remember its original shape. If you bend it and then heat it, it returns to its old shape as if by magic. Such metals are used in medicine, construction and engineering.
wichtigste: Shape-memory alloys return to an imprinted shape when heated.
The best-known shape-memory alloy is called nitinol and is made of nickel and titanium.
The effect is based on a change between martensite and austenite in the crystal lattice.
With pseudoelasticity, nitinol can be stretched by several per cent and springs back immediately.
With the two-way effect, a component switches between two shapes when heated and cooled.
Nitinol stents for blood vessels unfold by themselves inside the body.
Empa has developed a shape-memory steel that can be used to prestress concrete.
Copper zinc aluminium alloys also show a shape-memory effect.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is a mixture of several metals. Shape-memory alloys have an amazing property: they remember a shape that is imprinted on them when they are made. If you bend such a wire at room temperature and then heat it, it returns to its imprinted shape. That is why they are also called **memory metals**. The best known is **nitinol**, made of nickel and titanium.

The atoms in a metal are arranged in a regular **crystal lattice**. In shape-memory alloys, this lattice can have two different arrangements. At lower temperature the bendable form, **martensite**, is present; at higher temperature the rigid form, **austenite**. When heated, the lattice flips into austenite, and the component takes on its original shape again. The temperature at which this happens is called the transformation temperature.

With the **one-way effect**, a bent part returns to its shape once when heated and stays that way. With the **two-way effect**, the component switches back and forth between two shapes again and again as it is heated and cooled. Above the transformation temperature nitinol shows **pseudoelasticity**. It can then be stretched by several per cent and springs back immediately when released, much more than normal steel. This is used, for example, for very flexible spectacle frames.

A **stent** is a small mesh tube that keeps a narrowed blood vessel open. Nitinol stents are pushed into the vessel squashed together. The warmth of the body makes them unfold there by themselves to the right size. Brace wires made of nitinol also use the effect, because they press gently and evenly on the teeth.

At **Empa**, the research institute in Dübendorf, a shape-memory steel based on iron, manganese and silicon has been developed. It is much cheaper than nitinol and is suitable for construction. Bars of this steel are placed in concrete parts and then heated. Because they try to contract as they do so, they prestress the concrete and make it stronger. In this way old bridges, for example, can be strengthened afterwards.

The shape-memory effect was first observed in the 1930s in gold cadmium alloys. It became really well known in the early 1960s with the discovery of nitinol in a US Navy laboratory. The name nitinol stands for nickel, titanium and Naval Ordnance Laboratory. Besides nickel titanium, alloys of **copper, zinc and aluminium** also show a shape-memory effect.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mixture of two or more metals.
Shape-memory alloy made of nickel and titanium.
The bendable crystal form at lower temperature.
The rigid crystal form at higher temperature.
Small mesh tube that keeps a blood vessel open.

gewusst: A bent nitinol wire straightens out by itself in hot water.
Spectacle frames made of nitinol can be bent a lot without breaking.
Empa's shape-memory steel has already been used in Switzerland to strengthen bridges and buildings.

teile.einleitung: A combination lock is a lock that you open without a key by setting a secret number code. Usually you turn small wheels with the digits 0 to 9. Combination locks secure bikes, suitcases, lockers and safes.
wichtigste: A combination lock only opens when the right code is set.
Each wheel usually shows the digits 0 to 9.
One wheel on its own gives 10 possible codes.
With 3 wheels there are 1000 codes, from 000 to 999.
Each extra wheel multiplies the number of codes by ten.
After 9, a wheel goes back to 0.
Combination locks are a popular subject for maths puzzles.

abschnitte.text: Inside a combination lock, behind each wheel there is a disc with a **notch**. Only when all the wheels show the right digit do all the notches line up. Then the shackle or bolt can slide through and the lock opens. If even one wheel is wrong, it stays locked.

A code with three wheels is a three-digit number. So the code 200 + 30 + 4 is 234. If you turn the last wheel of 0 4 7 on by one, the lock shows 048. After 9 a wheel jumps back to 0, similar to a car’s **mileometer**.

A wheel with the digits 0 to 9 has 10 possibilities. With two wheels there are 10 · 10 = 100 codes, with three wheels 1000 and with four wheels already 10,000. This kind of calculation with possibilities is called **combinatorics**. The more wheels there are, the longer it would take to try all the codes.

For a **bike**, cable locks or D-locks with wheels are often used. Suitcases often have built-in combination locks with three digits. Safes often have a dial that you turn alternately left and right. Modern locks have a keypad, as on hotel safes or front doors.

A good code should not be easy to guess. Thieves try codes such as 000, 123 or your own year of birth first. After locking, you should turn the wheels so that nobody can read off the code. It is best to remember the code or write it down in a safe place.

Combination locks are a popular feature in **escape rooms** and brain-teasers. One example: three identical digits add up to 6, so the code is 222. Or the code is made of 1, 2 and 3 from the largest to the smallest digit, so 321. Puzzles like this train place value, calculation and logical thinking.

begriffe.erklaerung: A secret sequence of numbers or characters that opens or unlocks something.
A ring on the lock that can be turned, with the digits 0 to 9 on it.
A part of mathematics that counts how many possibilities there are.
An especially strong cupboard in which valuables are kept safely.

gewusst: If you tried one code every second on a lock with 4 wheels, you would need almost three hours for all 10,000 codes.
The code directly after 99 is 100, but for that you need a lock with at least three wheels.
In German the combination lock is called a “number lock” (Zahlenschloss).

teile.einleitung: A gas turbine is a machine that sucks in air, compresses it, burns it with fuel and uses the hot gases to drive a turbine wheel. It powers aircraft and produces electricity in power stations. In 1939 the Swiss company Brown, Boveri & Cie. built the first gas turbine for generating electricity, in Neuchâtel.
wichtigste: In a gas turbine the air flows through the compressor, combustion chamber and turbine.
The reference process of the gas turbine is called the Joule cycle (Brayton cycle).
In 1939 Brown, Boveri & Cie. built the first gas turbine for generating electricity, in Neuchâtel.
A higher pressure ratio in the compressor increases efficiency.
The hottest turbine blades are usually made of nickel-based superalloys.
The front blades are cooled inside with air, because the gas is hotter than their melting point.
In combined cycle power stations, the exhaust gases also produce steam for a steam turbine.
Such combined cycle power stations reach an electrical efficiency of over 60 per cent.

abschnitte.text: A gas turbine is a **heat engine** that converts heat into rotation. It consists of three main parts: the **compressor**, the combustion chamber and the turbine. All of them sit on a shared shaft that turns very fast. Unlike a car engine, it does not work in separate strokes but continuously. The fuel is usually natural gas, kerosene or heating oil.

First the compressor sucks in air and squeezes it together strongly. In the **combustion chamber**, fuel is injected and burned, producing very hot gas. This gas flows through the **turbine** and sets its blades turning. The turbine drives the compressor and also a generator or propeller. Experts describe this sequence with the **Joule cycle**.

The gas in modern gas turbines is hotter than the melting point of the turbine blades. That is why the front blades are cooled from inside with air flowing through tiny channels. The blades are usually made of **nickel-based superalloys**, which stay strong even in great heat. Often they are also coated with a ceramic protective layer. The hotter the gas and the higher the pressure ratio in the compressor, the better the efficiency.

The company **Brown, Boveri & Cie.** from Baden, BBC for short, built the first gas turbine for generating electricity in 1939. It was installed in Neuchâtel and supplied emergency power for the city there. Its output was about 4 megawatts. Today this machine is considered an important monument of the history of technology. BBC later became part of the ABB group.

The exhaust gases of a gas turbine are still very hot. In a **combined cycle gas and steam power station**, they produce steam in a boiler. This steam drives a second turbine, a steam turbine. In this way the energy in the fuel is used much better. Modern combined cycle power stations reach an electrical efficiency of over 60 per cent.

The **jet engines** of aircraft are also gas turbines. In them, a large part of the energy is used to push a fast jet of air out backwards. This creates the thrust that drives the aircraft forwards. Helicopters and propeller aircraft use gas turbines that turn the rotor or propeller via a shaft. Some ships are also powered by gas turbines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Part that sucks in air and squeezes it together strongly.
Space in which the fuel is burned with the air.
Idealised sequence used to calculate a gas turbine.
Share of the energy that is converted into useful work.
Especially heat-resistant metal mixture, often nickel-based.

gewusst: The gas in a modern gas turbine is hotter than the melting point of its own blades.
The world's very first gas turbine for generating electricity stood in Neuchâtel.
An aircraft engine is basically a gas turbine.

teile.einleitung: An exchange rate tells you how much one currency is worth in another. If you go on holiday to Italy or Austria, you exchange Swiss francs for euros and need the exchange rate to do so. Exchange rates change all the time, depending on how much demand there is for a currency.
wichtigste: The exchange rate shows how much one currency costs in another.
The Swiss franc has the international code CHF.
In Austria, Germany, France and Italy people pay with the euro.
To convert, you multiply the amount by the rate.
Exchange rates change through supply and demand.
When exchanging, banks charge a slightly worse rate so that they make money from it.
A strong franc makes holidays abroad cheaper.

abschnitte.text: Every country or group of countries has its own **currency**. Switzerland and Liechtenstein pay with the Swiss franc, code **CHF**. Many countries of the European Union use the euro, the USA the US dollar and Japan the yen. The **exchange rate** tells you how many units of one currency you get for one unit of the other.

Suppose 1 euro costs 0.95 francs; then 40 euros cost 40 times 0.95, that is 38 francs. If you get 1.05 euros for 1 franc, you get 210 euros for 200 francs. If 1 US dollar costs 0.80 francs, a T-shirt for 25 dollars costs 20 francs. If you get 170 yen for 1 franc, an ice cream costing the equivalent of 3 francs costs 510 yen.

Banks and **bureaux de change** have two different rates. When buying euros you pay a little more, and when changing them back you get a little less. If the bank pays 0.90 francs per euro after the holidays, you get 45 francs for 50 euros. The bank keeps the difference between the two rates as its earnings. Exchanging cash is usually more expensive than paying by card.

Exchange rates are set on the **foreign exchange market**, where huge sums of money are traded every day. If many people want to buy francs, its value rises. The franc is regarded as a safe haven, so in uncertain times it often becomes stronger. The **Swiss National Bank** can influence the rate, for example by buying or selling foreign currency. From 2011 to 2015 it set a minimum rate of 1.20 francs per euro.

If the franc becomes stronger, you get more euros for one franc, and holidays in the euro area become cheaper for Swiss people. At the same time Swiss products become more expensive for customers abroad. This affects, for example, watch companies, machine builders and tourism in the mountains. A weak franc has the opposite effect: it helps the export industry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money you pay with in a country.
Money held in currencies of other countries.
A business where you exchange money into another currency.
Selling goods abroad.

gewusst: On 15 January 2015 the National Bank ended the minimum rate, and the franc became much stronger within minutes.
The euro was introduced in 1999; the coins and notes came into circulation in 2002.
Liechtenstein also pays with the Swiss franc.

teile.einleitung: Counting is one of the first things children learn in maths. When counting, you say the numbers in order and give each thing exactly one number. In this way you find out how many things there are.
wichtigste: When counting, each thing gets exactly one number.
The last number said tells you how many things there are altogether.
On both hands together you have 10 fingers.
A week has 7 days, a year has 12 months.
You can count forwards and backwards.
Instead of counting one by one, you can also count in steps of two, five or ten.
Tally charts help you keep track when counting.

abschnitte.text: Fingers are the oldest counting aid. On both hands together you have **10 fingers**. That is why we calculate in the decimal system today. Many children show their age with their fingers. By the way, in different countries people start counting on different fingers; in Switzerland it is usually the thumb.

When counting, you touch each thing once and say a number: one, two, three. You must not forget anything or count anything twice. The **last number** tells you how many there are. It does not matter in what order you count; the result stays the same. The word “school”, for example, has **6 letters**.

When counting forwards, each number gets one bigger. When **counting backwards**, it gets one smaller. If Lena counts 10, 9, 8, 7, she says 6 next. You count backwards, for example, in the **countdown** before a rocket launch or on New Year’s Eve. People also often count when playing hide-and-seek.

Sometimes it is quicker to count in groups. A hen has 2 legs, so 3 hens together have 2, 4, 6 legs. A bike has 2 wheels, so 2 bikes have 4 wheels. In **steps of five** you count 5, 10, 15, 20. Such sequences help later with the **times tables**.

We count all the time without noticing. A week has **7 days**, from Monday to Sunday. A year has **12 months** and 365 days, or 366 in a leap year. When shopping you count coins and notes. In sport you count goals, points or laps.

Even in the Stone Age people scratched notches into bones or wood to count something. In Switzerland **tally sticks** were used for a long time, for example to record debts or quantities of milk. That is where the German expression “etwas auf dem Kerbholz haben” (“to have something on the tally stick”) comes from. Today people often make a **tally chart**, in which every fifth line goes across the other four. The abacus, a counting board with beads, also helped with counting.

begriffe.erklaerung: A list in which you make a line for each thing counted.
Counting backwards to zero, for example before a launch.
A wooden stick into which notches were cut in the past for counting.
A counting board with beads that can be moved.

gewusst: Some animals, such as crows and bees, can tell small amounts apart and can, in a way, count.
If you say one number every second without a break, you need more than eleven days to count to a million.
The German words “elf” and “zwölf”, like the English “eleven” and “twelve”, originally meant something like “one left over” and “two left over”.

teile.einleitung: An electric car does not run on petrol or diesel but on electricity from a large battery. An electric motor drives the wheels, quietly and with no exhaust fumes from the exhaust pipe. In Switzerland you see more of these cars on the roads every year.
wichtigste: An electric car stores its energy in a battery and drives the wheels with an electric motor.
Electric motors reach an efficiency of over 90 per cent, petrol engines only about a third of that.
An inverter converts the direct current from the battery into three-phase current for the motor.
When braking, the motor can work as a generator and send electricity back into the battery.
It is charged at a socket, at a wallbox or at a rapid charger.
From about 80 per cent full, a rapid charger charges much more slowly to protect the battery cells.
Electric cars produce no exhaust fumes while driving, but for their environmental impact it also matters how the electricity is generated.

abschnitte.text: The heart of an electric car is the **battery**, usually made of many lithium-ion cells. It often lies flat in the floor of the car, which makes the vehicle stable. Many manufacturers use batteries with a nickel manganese cobalt cathode, but more and more also use **lithium iron phosphate batteries** (LFP). LFP batteries need no cobalt and last a very long time. A battery management system monitors every cell so that it does not get too hot or too deeply discharged.

Many electric cars have a **permanent magnet synchronous motor**, which works very efficiently with magnets in its rotating part. The battery supplies direct current, but the motor needs three-phase current. This conversion is done by the **inverter**. Because the motor has its full power right from the start, electric cars often accelerate very quickly. A gearbox with many gears is usually not needed.

abschnitte.titel: Charging at home and on the road
abschnitte.text: At home people usually charge at a **wallbox** on the garage wall. With 11 kilowatts of charging power, it takes about 5 hours to add 55 kilowatt hours. At a **rapid charger** on the motorway it is much faster, often half an hour from low to 80 per cent. After that the battery management system lowers the current to protect the cells. That is why on a journey it is often worth charging only to about 80 per cent.

Consumption is measured in **kilowatt hours** per 100 kilometres. A car that uses 18 kWh per 100 km and has 72 kWh in its battery can travel roughly 400 kilometres. One kilowatt hour equals 3.6 megajoules of energy. A litre of petrol contains about 9 kWh, so a consumption of 15 kWh corresponds to only about 1.7 litres of petrol. In winter the range drops, because the cold slows the battery down and the heating uses electricity.

Electric cars are older than many people think. As early as around 1900, many electric vehicles were driving in cities such as Paris, London and New York. Then petrol cars won out, because they could travel further and petrol was cheap. Only with powerful **lithium-ion batteries** did electric cars come back from about 2010. Today almost all major car manufacturers build electric models.

In Switzerland in 2024, roughly one in five new cars sold was a fully electric car. Here the electricity comes largely from **hydropower** and nuclear power, so with little CO2. Many municipalities, shopping centres and motorway service areas offer charging stations. Anyone with their own home and a solar system can even charge their car with their own solar power.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rechargeable energy store, like a big mobile phone battery.
Recovering energy when braking; the motor becomes a generator of electricity.
A component that converts direct current into alternating or three-phase current.
A charging station on the wall, usually in the garage or at a parking space.
A unit of energy, abbreviated kWh.

gewusst: Around 1900, American cities at times had more electric cars than petrol cars.
An electric motor has far fewer moving parts than a petrol engine and needs no oil change.
With good driving and lots of regenerative braking, you need to use the brakes of an electric car much less often.

teile.einleitung: The numbers up to 100 include all the numbers from 0 to 100. Here children learn that numbers are made of tens and units and how to read, write and order them. It is an important step after the numbers up to 20.
wichtigste: Up to 100 there are one-digit numbers, two-digit numbers and 100.
The smallest two-digit number is 10, the largest is 99.
100 is made up of 10 tens.
In two-digit numbers the tens are on the left and the units on the right.
In German the units are said first, for example “siebenundvierzig” (seven and forty) for 47.
If you count from 1 to 100, you say exactly 100 numbers.
The hundred square and the hundred dot field help you get an overview of the numbers.

abschnitte.text: Every two-digit number is made up of **tens** and **units**. The number 47 has 4 tens and 7 units, that is 40 + 7. The place of a digit decides its value: the 4 in 47 means forty, but the 4 in 74 only four. The number 100 is made up of 10 tens, that is exactly one hundred.

In German two-digit numbers are said the other way round: for 63 you first say the three and then the sixty, “dreiundsechzig” (three and sixty). But when writing, the tens come first. That is why **swapped digits** often happen in dictation in German, for example 36 instead of 63. In French or English, on the other hand, you say the tens first, as in sixty-three.

The **hundred square** arranges the numbers from 1 to 100 in ten rows of ten numbers each. In each column all the numbers have the same units digit, and in each row almost all have the same tens digit. The hundred dot field shows 100 dots in a square, and on the bead frame you move beads. Wooden tens rods and unit cubes also make numbers something you can touch.

You can count forwards and backwards, in steps of one, two, five or ten. In steps of five it goes 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and so on. These **number sequences** are the basis for the times tables. If you can count quickly in steps of ten, you will later find sums such as 34 + 20 easy to do in your head.

Swiss money is good for practice. If you have 4 ten-franc notes and 6 one-franc coins, you have 46 francs. A hundred-franc note is worth as much as ten ten-franc notes or a hundred one-franc coins. When shopping and counting pocket money, you need the numbers up to 100 all the time.

In Switzerland children usually learn the numbers up to 100 in their second year at school. They practise comparing numbers, putting them in order and marking them on the number line. Then come addition and subtraction sums, first without and then with **crossing the ten**. After that they move on to the numbers up to 1000.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of ten units, in the left-hand place of a two-digit number.
The digit on the far right of a number; it counts the single pieces.
A table with the numbers from 1 to 100 in ten rows.
Going past a whole ten when calculating, for example in 38 + 5.

gewusst: From 10 to 99 there are exactly 90 two-digit numbers.
In the hundred square, all the numbers of the five times table are in just two columns.
In French-speaking Switzerland people say “septante” for 70, but in France “soixante-dix”, that is sixty-ten.

teile.einleitung: A dishwasher is a household appliance that washes plates, glasses, cutlery and pans automatically. In Switzerland people often simply say “Abwaschmaschine” or “Geschirrspüler”. It saves time and usually even uses less water than washing up by hand.
wichtigste: A dishwasher washes dishes automatically.
Rotating spray arms spray the water around inside.
Salt makes the water softer.
Rinse aid makes sure glasses dry without spots.
Glasses go in the top basket.
You scrape large food leftovers off the plate first.
A wooden board is better kept out of the machine.
A modern machine usually uses less water than washing up by hand.

abschnitte.text: A dishwasher is a cabinet with a watertight door in which dishes are cleaned with hot water and **detergent**. Inside there are usually two baskets and often a drawer for cutlery. A programme controls how long and how hot the wash is. Then the dishes are rinsed and dried. Most machines are built into the kitchen.

First the bottom of the machine fills with water, which is warmed by a **heater**. A pump pushes the water through rotating **spray arms**, which spray it forcefully onto the dishes. The water falls back, is filtered through a sieve and used again. At the end the machine pumps out the dirty water and rinses with fresh water. The **rinse aid** is added at this point so that glasses dry without spots.

In many areas of Switzerland the tap water is **hard**, which means it contains a lot of limescale. Limescale leaves white spots and can damage the machine. That is why it has a softener, for which you fill in special **dishwasher salt**. The salt makes the water softer. Table salt from the kitchen is not suitable for this.

You scrape large food leftovers into the bin first; you usually do not need to rinse the dishes. Glasses and cups go in the **top basket**, plates and pans at the bottom. The openings of cups and bowls point downwards so that no water stays in them. Wooden boards, wooden spoons, sharp knives and some plastic items do not belong in the machine. Wood swells in hot water and cracks.

In 1886 the American **Josephine Cochrane** patented a dishwasher. She wanted her fine china to stop breaking during washing up. At first it was mainly hotels and restaurants that bought such machines. In many households they only became common from the 1960s. In Switzerland, for example, the company V-ZUG in Zug builds dishwashers.

A modern dishwasher usually uses **less water** than washing up by hand under running water. You save most when the machine is full. An **eco programme** washes at a lower temperature and takes longer, but uses less electricity. The energy label shows how economical an appliance is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rotating arm that sprays the water onto the dishes.
Product that makes glasses dry without spots.
Special salt for the machine's water softener.
How much limescale is dissolved in the water.
Economy programme that uses less electricity and water.

gewusst: The inventor Josephine Cochrane mainly wanted to stop her china from breaking.
A full machine often uses only about as much water as two buckets.
The eco programme takes longer but still saves energy, because the water does not need to be as hot.

teile.einleitung: A television is a device that receives and shows moving pictures and sound. The German word “Fernsehen” actually means “seeing into the distance”, and the word television means the same, because you can see things happening far away. Since the 1950s there has been a television in many living rooms.
wichtigste: The word television means “seeing into the distance”.
In 1926 John Logie Baird was one of the first to show moving television pictures, in London.
The first televisions showed only black-and-white pictures.
A screen is made of tiny picture dots, the pixels.
With the remote control you can change channels comfortably from the sofa.
The radio and television broadcaster of German-speaking Switzerland is known as SRF.
In 1969 millions of people watched the Moon landing live on television.

abschnitte.text: A camera records pictures and breaks them down into many small dots. This information is sent to the television by cable, satellite, aerial or internet. The screen puts a picture back together from millions of tiny **pixels**. Each pixel is made of red, green and blue parts, from which all colours are mixed. Because many pictures are shown every second, you see smooth **movement**.

In 1926 the Scot **John Logie Baird** was one of the first to show moving television pictures, in London. The first pictures were small, blurred and black and white. In Switzerland a trial service with television broadcasts started in 1953. **Colour television** arrived in Switzerland at the end of the 1960s. Later flat screens replaced the heavy cathode-ray tube televisions.

On 21 July 1969 millions of people all over the world watched the **Moon landing** live on television. Very many people also watch the Olympic Games and football World Cups at the same time. A **live broadcast** is transmitted at exactly the moment it happens. In this way people on different continents can experience the same event together.

In Switzerland there are channels in several national languages. **SRF** is the radio and television of German-speaking Switzerland, RTS broadcasts in French and RSI in Italian. They all belong to the **SRG**. Households pay a fee for this so that there are programmes in all parts of the country. Well-known programmes include the “Tagesschau” news or children's programmes from SRF Kids.

Today many people watch films and series over the internet; this is called **streaming**. You can decide for yourself when to watch something. Modern televisions are often called smart TVs because they are connected to the internet. The **remote control** has existed since the 1950s. Too much television can make you tired, so it is good to take breaks and move about.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny picture dot on a screen.
A programme shown at exactly the moment it happens.
Playing films or music directly over the internet.
The Swiss Broadcasting Corporation, to which SRF, RTS and RSI belong.

gewusst: Old cathode-ray tube televisions were so heavy that it often took two people to carry them.
A modern 4K television has over 8 million pixels.
The pictures of the 1969 Moon landing were transmitted to Earth via aerials in Australia and the USA.

teile.einleitung: A bicycle dynamo is a small generator that produces electricity for the bike light while you ride. The energy for it comes from the force with which you push the pedals. That way you always have light, even without a battery.
wichtigste: The dynamo produces electricity for the bike light.
Its energy comes from the cyclist's pedalling.
With the dynamo switched on, you have to pedal a little harder.
A hub dynamo is built into the centre of the front wheel.
A bike light with a standlight keeps shining for a while after you stop.
The light at the front of a bicycle must be white.
Many people like to ride with lights on during the day too, because they are seen better.
In 1866 Werner Siemens discovered how to produce a strong current with a machine by turning it.

abschnitte.text: A dynamo is a small **generator**. Inside it, a magnet turns close to coils of wire. Through **induction** this creates an electrical voltage that makes the light shine. The faster you ride, the faster the magnet turns and the more current flows.

The classic **sidewall dynamo**, also called a bottle dynamo, sits on the fork and is flipped against the tyre with a small wheel. In the wet it can sometimes slip. The **hub dynamo** is built into the centre of the front wheel and works almost invisibly and reliably. It always turns, but brakes you hardly noticeably.

Modern bike lamps use economical **light-emitting diodes**. Many have a **standlight**: a small store is charged while you ride, and the light keeps shining for a while when you stop at a junction. That way you stay visible even while waiting. With the dynamo switched on you have to pedal a little harder, because the energy for the light comes from your own legs.

In Switzerland the light at the front of a bicycle must be **white** and at the back **red**. In the dark and in poor visibility you must ride with lights. Many people also ride with lights during the day, because they are then seen better. For e-bikes in Switzerland, lights are even compulsory during the day.

In 1866 **Werner Siemens** discovered how to produce a strong current with a machine by turning it. He called his principle dynamo-electric, which is where the word **dynamo** comes from. Bike lamps first used candles, oil or carbide gas. Later dynamos won out, because they reliably provide light without fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small generator that makes electricity from rotation.
Dynamo built into the wheel hub in the centre of the wheel.
Feature that keeps the bike light shining for a while after you stop.
The creation of voltage by a moving magnet close to a coil.

gewusst: The word dynamo comes from the Greek word for power.
A hub dynamo always turns, even when the light is switched off.
Bike lamps used to shine with carbide gas, which burned with a small flame.

teile.einleitung: EPFL, the École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne, is one of Switzerland's two Federal Institutes of Technology. Its large campus lies on Lake Geneva in the municipality of Ecublens near Lausanne. People from all over the world research and study here in engineering, natural sciences and architecture.
wichtigste: EPFL's main campus is in the municipality of Ecublens near Lausanne.
EPFL grew out of the École spéciale de Lausanne, founded in 1853.
The Rolex Learning Center was designed by the Japanese architecture firm SANAA and opened in 2010.
The Blue Brain Project started in 2005 and aimed to recreate the brains of mammals digitally.
EPFL students built SwissCube, the first Swiss satellite, which was launched into space in 2009.
The Swiss Plasma Center runs the TCV tokamak for fusion research.
EPFL has sites in Sion for energy research and in Neuchâtel (Microcity) for microengineering.

abschnitte.text: EPFL is a federal institute of technology and, like **ETH Zurich**, belongs to the ETH Domain. Teaching is mainly in French and English. Students here learn, for example, computer science, mechanical engineering, physics, biology or **architecture**. EPFL is one of the best-known technical universities in Europe.

Its roots go back to the **École spéciale de Lausanne** of 1853, a private engineering school. Later it became part of the University of Lausanne. In 1969 the Confederation took over the school, and it became the Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. In the following decades it moved to the new campus in **Ecublens** on Lake Geneva.

The campus lies right on the shore of Lake Geneva with a view of the Alps. The best-known building is the **Rolex Learning Center**, a library and place of learning with wavy floors and round courtyards. It was designed by the Japanese architecture firm **SANAA** and opened in 2010. The University of Lausanne is right next to EPFL.

In 2009 **SwissCube** was launched into space, the first Swiss satellite, built by EPFL students. It was a cube with edges only about ten centimetres long. The **Blue Brain Project**, started in 2005, aimed to recreate the brains of mammals digitally using supercomputers. The Swiss Plasma Center houses the **TCV tokamak**, which is used to research how energy could be obtained from nuclear fusion.

Besides Lausanne, EPFL is active in other places in French-speaking Switzerland. In **Sion** in Valais, the main focus is energy research. The **Microcity** site in Neuchâtel specialises in microengineering, fitting for the watchmaking region. There are further branches in Fribourg and Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: Grounds of a university with lecture halls, laboratories and libraries.
Ring-shaped device in which very hot gas is contained for fusion research.
Craft that orbits the Earth in space.
The joining together of atomic nuclei, as happens in the sun.

gewusst: The first Swiss satellite, SwissCube, was hardly bigger than a Rubik's Cube.
In the Rolex Learning Center there are almost no stairs; the floors rise like gentle hills.
In the TCV tokamak, gas is heated to temperatures hotter than the inside of the sun.

teile.einleitung: Photography is the art and technique of capturing lasting pictures with light. The word comes from Greek and means “drawing with light”. For almost 200 years people have used it to capture memories, events and the beauty of the world.
wichtigste: Photography means “drawing with light”.
Around 1826 Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest surviving photograph in the world.
The daguerreotype process, presented in 1839, is named after Louis Daguerre.
The camera obscura is a dark room into which an image of the outside world falls through a small hole.
In a simple pinhole camera the picture is upside down.
In digital cameras an image sensor replaces the film of the past.
The aperture controls how much light passes through the lens.

abschnitte.text: More than 2,000 years ago scholars already knew that light passing through a small hole throws an image onto a wall. Such a dark room is called a **camera obscura**, Latin for “dark chamber”. The image is upside down, because the light rays cross in the hole. Painters used the camera obscura to copy landscapes accurately. But it could not yet capture the image.

Around 1826 the Frenchman **Nicéphore Niépce** made the oldest surviving photograph in the world, a view from his window. For this the plate had to be exposed for many hours. His partner Louis Daguerre developed a better process, the **daguerreotype**, which was presented in Paris in 1839. Each daguerreotype was a one-off on a metal plate. Soon many people had their portraits taken in photo studios.

The Englishman William Henry Fox Talbot invented a process with a **negative**, from which many prints could be made. In 1888 the company Kodak brought out a simple camera with roll film. Now ordinary people could take photographs too, and the film was then developed in a laboratory. Colour films became widespread from the 1930s. For a long time families stuck their photos in photo albums.

The **lens** of a camera focuses the light and creates a sharp image. The **aperture** controls how much light passes through the lens, rather like the pupil in the eye. The shutter decides how long light comes in, the exposure time. In the past the light fell on a light-sensitive film. Today an **image sensor** measures the light and stores the picture as a file.

A digital photo consists of many picture dots, the pixels. A photo of 4,000 by 3,000 pixels has 12 million picture dots, that is 12 **megapixels**. Most photos today are taken with a smartphone. With image editing, photos can be changed, so you should not trust every picture on the internet. Anyone who photographs other people and publishes the pictures should ask for permission first.

begriffe.erklaerung: Dark chamber with a small hole through which an image of the outside world falls.
Early photographic process by Louis Daguerre with pictures on metal plates.
Picture in which light and dark are reversed and from which prints are made.
One million picture dots.
How long light falls on the film or sensor.

gewusst: For the oldest surviving photograph, the plate had to be exposed for so long that the sun moved across the sky in that time.
People rarely smile in early photos, partly because they had to keep still for a long time.
Today billions of photos are taken worldwide every day.

teile.einleitung: The bicycle, in Switzerland usually called a “Velo”, is a vehicle with two wheels that you drive with your own muscle power using pedals. It is quiet, healthy and needs no petrol. Worldwide there are more bicycles than cars.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people usually call a bicycle a “Velo”.
A normal bicycle has two wheels.
In 1817 Karl Drais invented the running machine, the forerunner of the bicycle.
The first running machine did not yet have pedals.
When cycling you should wear a bike helmet.
At the back of a bicycle a red light shines, at the front a white one.
Cycling is good for your health and for the environment.

abschnitte.text: A bicycle consists of a **frame**, two wheels, handlebars and a saddle. With your feet you push the **pedals**, which drive the back wheel via a chain. Gears help you get up steep roads too. With brakes on the handlebars you can stop safely. In Switzerland lights, reflectors and a bell are part of the required equipment.

In 1817 the German **Karl Drais** invented the running machine in Mannheim, also called the draisine. It had two wheels but no pedals yet; you pushed yourself along the ground with your feet. Around 1860 bicycles in France got pedals on the front wheel. After that came penny-farthings with a huge front wheel. Around 1885 the safety bicycle with a chain drive appeared, which already looked almost like today's bicycles.

A **bike helmet** protects your head in a fall. A red light must shine at the back and a white one at the front so that you can be seen well at dusk. Anyone who cycles must know the rules of the road, such as hand signals when turning. In Switzerland many children take a **cycling test** at school. On cycle paths and cycle lanes you are safer, separated from the cars.

There are **mountain bikes** for forest tracks, racing bikes for fast rides on the road and city bikes for town. An **e-bike** has an electric motor that helps when you pedal. With cargo bikes you can carry shopping or even children. Tandems have room for two people, one behind the other. Children often first learn to ride on a balance bike without pedals, just like Drais's invention.

Switzerland has a dense network of signposted cycle routes, which you can recognise by red signposts. The **SwitzerlandMobility** project shows many of these routes on a map. Especially in cities such as Basel, Bern or Winterthur, many people cycle to work or school every day. Cycling makes no noise, causes no exhaust fumes and keeps you fit.

begriffe.erklaerung: Karl Drais's running machine without pedals, the forerunner of the bicycle.
Part with which you can make pedalling easier or harder.
Old bicycle with a very large front wheel.
Bicycle with an electric motor that helps when you pedal.

gewusst: Karl Drais's running machine is said to have been invented when horses were scarce because of a famine.
Cycling is one of the most energy-efficient ways of moving under your own power.
Worldwide there are estimated to be more than a billion bicycles.

teile.einleitung: George de Mestral was a Swiss engineer who invented Velcro. He got the idea when he had to pick burrs out of his dog's fur after an outing. Today his invention is found in shoes, jackets and bags, and it has even been used in space travel.
wichtigste: George de Mestral came from Switzerland and was born in the canton of Vaud.
He studied in Lausanne and worked as an engineer.
After an outing, burrs were stuck in his dog's fur.
He examined the burrs closely with a microscope.
He had the idea for Velcro in 1941.
It took about ten years from the idea to the patent application.
He gave his invention the name Velcro.

abschnitte.text: George de Mestral was born in 1907 in the **canton of Vaud**. Even as a teenager he liked tinkering, and he applied for a patent for a toy aeroplane. He studied at the technical university in **Lausanne** and became an **engineer**. As well as technology, he was also interested in nature and hunting. He died in 1990 in French-speaking Switzerland.

In 1941 de Mestral came back from an outing with his dog. Many **burrs**, the seed heads of a plant, were stuck in the dog's fur and on his clothes. Instead of just being annoyed, he wanted to know why they stuck so well. Under the **microscope** he saw that the burrs have tiny hooks. These hooks get caught in hairs and loops of fabric.

De Mestral wanted to recreate this idea: one strip with lots of tiny hooks and a second with lots of tiny **loops**. If you press the two together, they hold firmly, and you can pull them apart again. When an invention copies nature, this is called **bionics**. Velcro is considered one of the best-known examples of it.

Putting it into practice was harder than expected. For many years de Mestral searched for the right material and a machine that could make the tiny hooks. Finally he found that **nylon** worked well. It took about ten years from the idea to the patent application. He called his invention **Velcro**, from the French words “velours” for velvet and “crochet” for hook.

Today Velcro fastenings are found on children's shoes, jackets, blood pressure cuffs and rucksacks. They have also been used in space travel to hold objects in place in weightlessness. The name Velcro is still a well-known brand today. George de Mestral is one of the most famous examples of Swiss inventiveness.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plant whose seed heads stick to fur and clothes with tiny hooks.
Fastening made of a strip of hooks and a strip of loops.
Official protection that secures an invention for its inventor for a certain time.
Technology that imitates ideas from nature.
Brand name for the hook-and-loop fastening, from “velours” and “crochet”.

gewusst: Velcro came about because someone wondered about burrs in a dog's fur instead of just being annoyed.
The name Velcro is made up of the French words for velvet and hook.
On space stations, Velcro strips help to hold objects in place in weightlessness.

teile.einleitung: Escher Wyss was a famous Zurich engineering company founded in 1805. It built steamships, turbines and machines and became known worldwide especially for equipment for hydropower stations. The Escher-Wyss-Platz in Zurich still recalls the company today.
wichtigste: Hans Caspar Escher and Salomon von Wyss founded the company in Zurich in 1805.
Escher Wyss started out with a mechanical spinning mill.
From 1835 the company built steamships that sailed on many lakes.
In 1856 Escher Wyss set up a branch in Ravensburg in southern Germany.
In 1860 the company closed its spinning mill, because engineering had become more important.
In the 20th century Escher Wyss was a world leader in equipment for hydropower stations.
In 1969 Sulzer took over the company.
The Escher-Wyss-Platz in Zurich's industrial district recalls the company.
